title: Opposition asks Supreme Court to let it put 48 questions to Election Commission on SIR
dek: Rahul Gandhi and other INDIA bloc leaders want sworn answers from the Chief Election Commissioner and both Election Commissioners on who authorised the voter-roll revision. The court hears the case on Tuesday.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and other leaders of the opposition INDIA bloc on Monday asked the Supreme Court for permission to put 48 written questions, known in law as interrogatories, to the Election Commission about how the nationwide Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls was decided and run, according to reports.

The application, filed in a pending case, asks that the answers be given on oath by the Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, by the two Election Commissioners, and by the Deputy Election Commissioner who signed the Commission's reply to the court. The court is scheduled to hear the petitions on Tuesday, 17 November.

## What the opposition wants to know

The questions, as reported, cover three areas: who authorised the SIR, how voters came to be excluded from the rolls, and what changes were made to the Commission's online systems. They ask whether the Chief Election Commissioner used the Commission's powers without the knowledge, approval or agreement of the other two Commissioners, and point to what the petitioners say is the absence of any recorded decision of the full Commission authorising a nationwide revision.

The application also asks about changes to the online version of Form 6, the form used to enrol new voters, and to ECINET and ERONET, the Commission's electoral databases, which the petitioners describe as centralised and opaque. It asks who carried out portal upgrades and who approved them, saying the Commission's reply did not identify them, according to reports.

Interrogatories are a procedure from civil litigation in which one side may, with the court's permission, require the other to answer written questions on oath. Courts grant them sparingly in petitions against constitutional bodies.

## What the Commission has said

In a 248-page reply filed on Saturday, the Commission defended the SIR. The affidavit, signed by Deputy Election Commissioner Bhanu Prakash Yeturu, said no changes had been made to the statutory Form 6 and that "the attempt to make aspersions against the Election Commission is unfortunate", according to reports. It said all three Commissioners had unanimously approved the affidavit, and that the SIR orders of 24 June 2025, 27 October 2025 and 14 May 2026 were issued by unanimous decisions under Article 324 of the Constitution and the 2023 law on the appointment and service conditions of Election Commissioners.

The same affidavit told the court that voters left off the draft rolls who reapply on Form 6 will not be prosecuted for having been enrolled before, and accepted that errors may have occurred in removing the names of dead and non-existent voters.

## Background

Mr Gandhi and 10 other INDIA bloc leaders filed their petition on 12 October, seeking, among other things, production of the Commission's internal records on the SIR, an independent audit of voter deletions and an interim suspension of the revision, according to reports. On 15 October a bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant asked the Commission and the Chief Election Commissioner to respond to petitions, including Mr Gandhi's, alleging large-scale deletions of voters and irregularities in the SIR. The petitions followed a newspaper report on 25 September that the two Election Commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had objected on record at least 14 times in 10 months to SIR decisions that, they said, had been issued without their knowledge or recommendation. The Commission's latest affidavit says the decisions were unanimous.

The SIR has been a running dispute between the government and the opposition since the revision began in Bihar in 2025, and it has been extended to other states since. The Commission says the revision is needed to remove ineligible and duplicate entries; opposition parties say eligible voters are being removed.

## What happens next

The Supreme Court will hear the petitions on Tuesday. It may decide whether to allow the interrogatories, ask the Commission to respond to the application, or take up the main challenge to the SIR directly.
